nodes.name: high-voltage electrical equipment manufacturers
nodes.mechanism: Utilities and data center developers order more power transformers, switchgear, and circuit breakers, creating multi-year backlogs and pricing power.
nodes.logic: Grid capex translates directly into demand for high-voltage equipment that has long lead times and concentrated supply. Producers can raise prices and choose higher-margin orders as demand exceeds capacity. Earnings are levered because a small increase in volume can drive a larger increase in operating margin.

nodes.name: grid engineering and construction services
nodes.mechanism: Utilities and developers award more transmission and substation engineering, procurement, and construction contracts.
nodes.logic: The buildout requires specialized design, permitting, and construction labor. As contract awards accelerate, EPC firms build backlog and gain negotiating power on terms. Margins can expand because scarce labor and equipment allow fixed-price contracts to be written with higher contingency and escalation clauses.

nodes.name: gas turbine and power generation equipment makers
nodes.mechanism: Data center developers and utilities order gas turbines for firm, fast-to-deploy power.
nodes.logic: Data center load growth requires around-the-clock power that cannot wait for long transmission upgrades. Gas turbines offer the shortest reliable path to new capacity, so orders rise ahead of general electricity demand. The effect is compounded by aftermarket service revenue tied to installed units.

nodes.name: large industrial electricity consumers
nodes.mechanism: Data center load raises wholesale power prices and allocated grid charges for existing industrial users.
nodes.logic: Data centers add demand in specific regions, tightening reserve margins and pushing up locational power prices. The grid capex needed to serve them is recovered through rates, adding a second layer of cost for industrial customers. Industrial users often cannot pass through these costs quickly, so operating margins shrink.

nodes.name: grain-oriented electrical steel suppliers
nodes.mechanism: Transformer manufacturers buy more grain-oriented electrical steel, raising volumes and prices for mills.
nodes.logic: Grain-oriented electrical steel is the core material in high-voltage transformers. Supply is concentrated and capacity additions are slow, while transformer backlogs grow. Mills can sell out and push through price increases, making earnings levered to the spread between electrical steel prices and input costs.

nodes.name: small municipal and cooperative utilities
nodes.mechanism: Small utilities pay higher prices and wait longer for distribution transformers and switchgear.
nodes.logic: Large investor-owned utilities place multi-year orders and get priority in production schedules. Municipal and cooperative buyers lack that scale and face equipment shortages that force them to delay maintenance or pay spot prices. Thin balance sheets and slower rate recovery make the cost increase more painful.

nodes.name: specialty high-voltage electrical contractors
nodes.mechanism: Contractors with high-voltage linemen and substation electricians see more hours, larger crews, and higher billable rates.
nodes.logic: The grid buildout is constrained by certified labor, not just materials. Contractors that can retain high-voltage crews can win more work and pass through wage increases. Revenue scales with hours worked, so these firms track grid capex directly and benefit from overtime and per diem charges.

nodes.name: renewable energy project developers
nodes.mechanism: Renewable developers face longer interconnection timelines and higher construction costs as grid resources shift toward data center load.
nodes.logic: Interconnection studies and network upgrades compete with data center transmission requests, slowing queue processing. EPC firms and equipment suppliers prioritize larger, higher-margin data center and grid reliability work. Renewable projects already burdened by interconnection backlogs see further delays, reducing returns and pushing some projects past viability.

nodes.name: gas turbine aftermarket service providers
nodes.mechanism: Owners of the expanding gas turbine fleet spend more on maintenance, parts, and performance upgrades.
nodes.logic: New gas turbine orders add to the installed base, generating recurring service revenue for decades. Data center backup and peaking units may run more hours than typical, accelerating maintenance intervals. Aftermarket work carries higher margins than original equipment and is less sensitive to new order cycles.

nodes.name: on-site generation and microgrid developers
nodes.mechanism: Industrial electricity consumers invest in on-site generation, storage, and microgrids to hedge grid power costs.
nodes.logic: Higher utility rates and reliability concerns make self-supply projects economically attractive. Gas engines, fuel cells, and batteries can reduce peak demand charges and provide backup during grid stress. This capex is incremental to grid spending and benefits niche equipment and project developers.

nodes.name: electrical steel processing and slitting services
nodes.mechanism: Electrical steel processors and slitters see higher volume and conversion fees.
nodes.logic: Mills often sell wide coils to processors that cut and slit electrical steel to lamination sizes for transformer OEMs. As transformer production ramps, processors add shifts and pass through higher conversion costs. Capacity is niche and regional, giving processors pricing power independent of steel prices.

nodes.name: grid equipment testing and commissioning services
nodes.mechanism: Independent testing and commissioning firms see rising demand for substation and protection system certification.
nodes.logic: Every new substation and transmission line must be tested before energization. As construction volume rises, utilities require third-party certification to manage risk and meet reliability standards. This work is scheduled late in the project cycle, so revenue follows construction with a lag.

nodes.name: renewable energy equipment suppliers
nodes.mechanism: Suppliers of solar modules, wind turbines, and inverters face order pushouts and pricing pressure as renewable projects slip.
nodes.logic: Delayed renewable projects postpone equipment deliveries and can trigger cancellation or renegotiation. In oversupplied markets for some components, further delays worsen capacity utilization and pricing. Suppliers with utility-scale exposure see revenue recognition shift later and margins compress.

nodes.name: distributed energy resource management software providers
nodes.mechanism: Providers of microgrid control and distributed energy resource software see larger deployments as on-site assets multiply.
nodes.logic: Industrial users that install generation, storage, and microgrids need software to optimize dispatch, islanding, and grid services. Software revenue is recurring and grows with the number of connected sites. This niche benefits from the installed base created by on-site power investment, so it scales faster than hardware installation alone.
